title: How to create a savings plan for buying your first home in the US
description: Reverse-engineering the down payment and closing costs for first-time buyers.
content:
Buying a home is the largest purchase most Americans will ever make. The price tag is daunting—saving $60,000 or $100,000 takes years of discipline. Many potential buyers fail because they don't have a concrete plan; they just vaguely 'save money' and hope it adds up. A successful House Fund strategy requires calculating the exact 'Cash to Close' number, choosing the right savings vehicle to protect that cash, and automating the monthly contribution. This guide turns the dream of homeownership into a math problem you can solve.

Key Takeaways

  • The Full Number: You need more than a Down Payment. You need Closing Costs (2-4%), Moving Expenses, and an 'Immediate Repair' buffer. Plan for the full stack.
  • Risk-Free Storage: House money needed in <3 years should NEVER be in the stock market. Use High-Yield Savings or Treasury Bills to protect the principal.
  • The 20% Myth: You can buy with 3.5% (FHA) or 3% (Conventional). While PMI adds cost, it allows you to enter the market 5-7 years sooner.
  • Automated Sinking Fund: Treat your house savings like a rent payment to your future self. It must be a fixed monthly bill.

Why It Matters (US Context)

First-time homebuyer programs vary by state. Many offer Down Payment Assistance (DPA) grants. Additionally, the IRS allows you to withdraw up to $10,000 of *earnings* from a Roth IRA penalty-free for a first home (plus all contributions). Knowing these rules accelerates the timeline.

Calculating Your 'Cash to Close'

Let's assume a target home price of $400,000.

Option A: The Gold Standard (20% Down)

  • Down Payment: $80,000
  • Closing Costs (3%): $12,000
  • Reserves: $5,000
  • Total Goal: $97,000

Option B: The Fast Track (3.5% Down)

  • Down Payment: $14,000
  • Closing Costs (3%): $12,000
  • Reserves: $5,000
  • Total Goal: $31,000

The Reality: Option B is achievable in 2 years saving $1,300/mo. Option A takes 6+ years. In rising markets, Option B is often smarter despite the PMI cost.

Where to Park the Cash

  1. Open a Dedicated Account: Do not mix this with your Emergency Fund. Open a specific HYSA named 'House Fund'.
  2. Maximize Yield: Use a Money Market Fund (e.g., Vanguard VMFXX) or T-Bills to get ~5% yield. On $30,000, that is $1,500/year in free money—enough to buy a new fridge.
  3. The 'Windfall' Rule: Commit 100% of tax refunds and work bonuses to the House Fund. This can cut your timeline by 30%.
  4. Audit Your Rent: Can you move to a cheaper apartment for 12 months? Saving the $500/mo difference adds $6,000 to the fund. Short-term pain for long-term gain.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I use my 401(k)?

Generally No. 401(k) loans are risky (if you lose your job, you must repay instantly). Hardship withdrawals come with taxes and penalties. Leave retirement money for retirement.

What if home prices drop?

If you are buying for the long term (7+ years), short-term drops don't matter. You are buying a place to live, not just an investment asset.

How do I avoid PMI?

Put 20% down. Or, put 10% down and take a 'Piggyback Loan' (80/10/10 structure). Or, just pay PMI for a few years until your equity grows, then refinance to remove it.
